prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: On re-reading the eight ballots I move B001 to first place in my own preferred configuration. It is the one candidate with a concrete, well-delimited achievement, a clean two-name credit and broad support across five different members' rankings, including four first places. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the Doppler, recoil and light-shift problems of trapped neutral atoms while keeping a very large atom number, and Ye's strontium clocks and clock comparisons took that scheme to the 10^-18 regime. Several laboratories now reproduce this performance, and the clocks are already used for relativistic geodesy, searches for variation of constants and dark-sector physics, and they underpin the planned redefinition of the second. This is not my own field, so I weigh it by the usual criteria of originality, demonstrated impact and clarity of attribution, and it does well on all three. My opening ranking placed B003 first, but I now think that ranking mixed scientific merit with familiarity, since cQED is the area I work in every day. I do not want my closeness to the subject to substitute for the comparative argument.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that atomic clocks have been recognised repeatedly (1989, 2005 for the comb, 2012 for ion control), so some members may see a further clock prize as incremental, and the two-name list leaves out other lattice-clock contributors such as Ludlow, Hinkley and the Paris group. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened. For my own opening first choice, B003, the case against is that it follows too closely on the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and the Blais versus Girvin allocation among four credited names cannot be settled cleanly with a three-person limit. B010 is intellectually the deepest alternative, but Hasan, Mele and the uncredited Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal make its attribution the least stable on the table.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B003 third but worries about returning to superconducting circuits so soon after the 2025 prize, and he places Halzen and IceCube first as a detector-led discovery of a new observational window.
responses.response: I agree with the timing concern and I will say so against my own opening ballot. Circuit QED is a different achievement from macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit, since it concerns strong light-matter coupling and dispersive readout, but a lay reader would not separate the two quickly, and the committee does not need to hurry. I disagree with Pearce on B027 as a preferred option. The astrophysical neutrino flux is firmly established, but source identification is still partial, and a one-name credit for a collaboration of this size is exactly the narrow configuration Danielsson also found hard to defend. I would keep it as a strong later candidate, not a lead.

responses.point: Lindroth puts the lattice clock first, regards the 2005 comb prize as complementary rather than overlapping, and notes that the credited names omit other contributors so fairness of a two-person split cannot be tested within the list.
responses.response: I find the complementarity argument persuasive. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, whereas the lattice clock solved the separate problem of interrogating many neutral atoms without systematic shifts from motion, and that is Katori's contribution and Ye's demonstration of its accuracy limits. I accept her caution about uncredited contributors, but every candidate on the shortlist has that problem and the two-name B001 credit has the smallest gap. Where I differ is on B003: she drops Girvin and keeps Blais, and I do not think that is as easy as her ballot suggests. I would not oppose Girvin over Blais if we ever took that candidate up, which is another reason I do not put it first.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first for its originality and metrology impact, but asks whether the 2005 Hall-Hansch prize already covers the frequency-comb side, and he regards the 2025 prize as making near-term recognition of circuit QED less likely.
responses.response: I agree on both points and they are linked. On the comb, Ye's earlier work with Hall's group does give some overlap in people, but the discovery credited here is the lattice clock, and the two-name list does not include Hall or Hansch, so the new prize would not duplicate the old citation. On circuit QED, Kroll is right that my opening support for B003 was the thinnest of any candidate I ranked first, with only two top-three placements. I would add that the right question for B001 is whether 10^-18 performance is independently confirmed, and it is, at JILA, RIKEN and several national metrology institutes.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a concrete prediction followed by a specific experiment, and he ranks the Higgs detector-conception candidate second while noting the attribution problem for collaboration-scale discoveries.
responses.response: I take his B017 argument seriously. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 experiments are a rare theory-experiment pair, and I ranked it sixth mainly for maturity reasons, because the pairing mechanism is still unresolved and the experimental first author is not in the credited names. I do not think eight years is too short in principle, but I would want that question settled before it displaces a candidate whose interpretation is stable. On B002 I share his hesitation about honouring spokespersons and project leaders rather than the discovery, and I would not put it in my own configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the clock first and the optical-lattice quantum simulator second, notes that any three-name selection from five credited names leaves out decisive contributors, and wonders whether B010 is too close to the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I share his view that B042 is a serious achievement, and I ranked it fifth. His own proposal of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller shows the allocation problem clearly, because the experimental and theoretical strands are separable but Cirac and Zoller also belong to the trapped-ion candidate B032. That interaction is a reason to keep B042 and B032 out of a lead position until we know how the committee wants to treat the Cirac-Zoller theory credit. On B010 I am less concerned about 2016 than he is, since topological insulators rest on the band topology of time-reversal-invariant systems, which is distinct from the topological phase transitions of that prize, but I agree the Mele versus Hasan choice for the third place is unresolved.

uncertainties: I cannot independently verify the finer history of the magic-wavelength proposal or the relative weight of Katori's concept against Ye's accuracy record, and this is outside my own research field.
Whether the committee regards the 2005 and 2012 prizes as leaving enough room for a further precision-measurement award is a judgement I cannot settle from the ballots alone.
Whether B003 should be taken up after the 2025 prize, and whether Girvin or Blais is the right third theorist, remains open. My own view is influenced by subject-matter familiarity.
The three-person limit leaves the attribution of B010 (Hasan, Mele and the uncredited Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal) and B042 (theory versus experiment) unstable.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict with any credited candidate is apparent from my profile. I direct WACQT and work in circuit and waveguide QED, the area of B003 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin), and Chalmers hosted researchers connected with the 2025 prize, so I disclose subject-matter proximity on B003 and would defer to the chair on recusal if the committee took that candidate up. No documented link to Katori, Ye or the other credited names is recorded.
